Bursting with heart and humor, the production showcases all of the intricacies and beauty of Black American life, the never-ending costs of slavery, racism and discrimination and how Black people flourish and move forward despite it all.
Allen’s production starts gently, as does the play, and it honors the other side of Wilson, which is to write about how Blacks found spaces, even in 1911, for humor and community with each other.

It is a credit to Wilson’s monumental talent, and the astuteness of this production, that we’re left at the end with the sense of a past that won’t fade and a future that might never know what to make of it.
Joe Turner is one of Wilson's most moving, mystical and musical plays.
And so the evening concludes with an explosion of emotion that redeems its flaws, and sends us reeling, shaken, into the night.
Wilson’s language rushes past and over every barrier.

The actor is the soul of this production, and deftly escapes its failings.
This “Joe Turner” comes alive instantly with arresting performances that only tighten their grip as the drama intensifies.
Of course, the blues sing most powerfully here in Wilson’s language, and the director and her performers play it with an authority that feels as effortless as it is potent.
Wilson does a wonderful job of showcasing a community of passersby who share a common identity.
What it mostly seems to lack is a reason for being.
Inhabited by this talented ensemble, it feels like each one of these characters could step off the stage into real life with the snap of a finger.
In director Debbie Allen's sturdy production of August Wilson's intense and lyrical play, Cedric The Entertainer and Taraji P. Henson portray the stable long-time married couple.
Wilson is one of the 20th Century’s most important dramatists and his plays, whenever they are on stage, demand we take notice.
In doing so, this August Wilson veteran also makes the case for the transformational power of theater, too.
The production’s central problem is not any single misstep but a lack of cohesion.
His turn as Bynum is a performance for the ages, and one that elevates every actor in his orbit.
Softness slides into sleepiness in this unremarkable revival, now at the Theatre, which never comes to life despite several intriguing performances.
That's what makes this particular return feel so compelling.

cn.t: Wilson's masterpiece receives a sturdy but uneven revival, with critics praising the ensemble cast (especially Ruben Santiago-Hudson) and the play's enduring power, though many find Debbie Allen's direction doesn't fully cohere.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.

vr.q: Overall, this was a great production of a somewhat understated but beautiful play about seeking identity, faith, and community in the wake of slavery.
